verses.translation_literal: A song for the ascents. I lift up my eyes to the mountains: from where will my help come?
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for the climbing. I lift my eyes, and the mountains stand there, ridge behind ridge, silent and enormous. Where, out of all that stone, is my help going to come from?
verses.directors_commentary:
Open on a person standing still on a road, head tilted back. The heading, "a song for the ascents," ties this psalm to a set of fifteen (Pss 120–134). Tradition links them to pilgrims going up to Jerusalem, and the Levites on the steps of the Temple (Rashi on Ps 121:1 gives the Levites). The Hebrew has "for the ascents," not "of"; Radak and Metzudat Zion take the lamed as standing in for the definite article, so "the ascents." The KJV's "degrees" is the old English for steps. It is accurate and nearly unreadable today.

The verse is not a boast of faith. The KJV and ASV make it "I will lift up mine eyes… from whence cometh my help," a confident statement. The Hebrew has two clauses and a question mark between them: I lift my eyes to the mountains. From where does help come? The question is open. Mountains in the ancient Near East were where gods lived and where the sanctuaries on high places stood, and they were also where bandits and enemy scouts appeared. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David hear a watcher, someone besieged or under attack, who climbs a height and scans for rescuers. Whether the speaker looks to the hills for hope or in dread is the actor's choice, and verse 2 answers it. Play the eyes before the words.

The pairing of "eyes" with "lift up" is the idiom nasa' 'einayim, to look up deliberately, as Abraham does when he sees the ram.

philological_notes.note: A compound of min, 'from', and 'ayin, 'where?', so 'from where?', a real question. It is the same word Jacob uses when he asks the shepherds of Haran "from where are you?" in Gen 29:4. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'from what place' and cites Gen 29. Ibn Ezra stresses that it is a question about the place the help comes from, and that the form is fixed. It is not the noun 'ayin, 'nothing', although the spelling is the same without the prefix.

'For the ascents'. The word is from the root 'lh, 'go up'. Whether it means steps, stages of a pilgrimage, a rising musical line or something else is not known. Rashi gives two readings: the Levites beginning to go up the steps, and, from the Sifrei, a song 'for the one who will make ascents for the righteous' in the future.

verses.translation_literal: My help [is] from with YHWH, maker of heaven and earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the answer comes, quiet and sure, the way a held breath lets go: my help is from the LORD, from the One who made the heavens and the earth. Not from the mountains. From the One who made them.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the reply, and it should land softly after the open question of verse 1. The first word of the verse, 'my help', is the last word of the previous verse: the Hebrew hands the word across the line break, so the answer picks up exactly where the question stopped. Keep that handover in the voice.

The preposition is מֵעִם, literally 'from with': help that comes out from beside someone, from a presence that stands near. The KJV 'from the Lord' loses the nearness. The phrase 'maker of heaven and earth' is a quiet challenge to the surrounding peoples, for whom mountains, sky and sun were gods or the thrones of gods. The singer has just looked at the mountains; now they are demoted to creatures, part of what YHWH made. The KJV 'which made' turns the participle עֹשֵׂה into a past-tense clause; the Hebrew is a title, 'maker of', a standing description of who YHWH is.

philological_notes.note: A compound of min 'from' and 'im 'with': from beside, from the side of. The help comes from someone present, not remote.
A participle, 'maker of', a title rather than a story. The same phrase 'heaven and earth' names the whole created order, mountains included.

verses.translation_literal: May he not give your foot to slipping; may he not slumber, your keeper.
verses.translation_dramatic: He will not let your foot slide on the loose stones. He who keeps you will not nod, will not drift into sleep, not once.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice changes. Verse 1 was "I"; verse 3 is "you." Someone answers, or the speaker turns and speaks to themselves, and the question of verse 1 has been taken from them. Malbim hears a voice that says: why look about for help as if it were news? Radak and Meiri hear one person consoling another, a fellow exile.

The verbs are jussive. אַל with the imperfect is the negative of a wish or command: "may he not give," "let him not." The KJV, ASV and YLT make both lines flat statements ("He will not suffer…"). That is not a mistranslation so much as an old reading: Ibn Ezra says אַל here is simply לֹא, and the Targum renders it with לָא, "not." So the KJV follows a very early reading of the form. The BBE keeps the wish, "May he not let your foot be moved." Either way it is a blessing, an assurance spoken to a traveller. If you play it as a wish, the actor is pressing a hand on someone's shoulder.

The Hebrew is physical. The foot goes to "the slipping" (mot, a stumble, a shaking), a word used for a foundation that gives way. Walking on a mountain path, in the dark or on rock after rain, this is a real danger. "Suffer" in the KJV is archaic for "allow." The Hebrew verb is literally "give," the same verb as in "give your foot to the slipping." The second line uses a rare word for sleep: num is the light drowse, not deep sleep (Metzudat Zion). The sentries on a city wall, Ibn Ezra notes, keep watch through the night. The guard who nods off is the ancient picture of failure, and the speaker says that this guard does not.

philological_notes.note: From the root mwt, 'totter, slip, be shaken'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as inclining and stumbling. It is used of feet that give way and of earth and mountains that shake (Ps 46:3), so a foot on a firm path is a small echo of a collapse of the world.

The negative of a wish or a prohibition, used with the jussive. Ibn Ezra reads it as equal to לֹא, 'not', and the Targum translates it with לָא, which is why the KJV has 'will not'. The sense is one of assurance either way.
'Slumber', from the root nwm. Metzudat Zion says it means a little, light sleep, a drowse. The word is used with sleep (yashen) in the next verse, so the sequence is from drowsing to deep sleep.

verses.translation_literal: Behold, he will not slumber and he will not sleep, keeper of Israel.
verses.translation_dramatic: Listen. He does not slumber, and he does not sleep, the Keeper of Israel. No lamp of his goes out in the night. The watch is never relieved, because it is never left.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice rises from a personal 'you' to a national 'Israel', and the key word 'keeper' is the one that rings through the whole psalm: the root שמר appears six times in these eight verses. Make the audience hear the repetition. The verse opens with הִנֵּה, 'behold', a word that points a finger. The KJV 'behold' is faithful here, and 'neither slumber nor sleep' is acceptable, though it turns two negatives into one 'neither/nor' construction and slightly dulls the double 'not' of the Hebrew.

The two verbs form a climb: slumber is the nod, sleep is full unconsciousness. Radak and Meiri both note that 'slumber' is lighter, so the line says: not even the lightest lapse, and certainly not deep sleep. There is also a sharp edge for a Near Eastern audience. In the neighbouring religions gods sleep and wake, and the prophets mock a god who may be asleep (1 Kings 18:27 does so of Baal). The Keeper of Israel does not need a night shift. Ibn Ezra adds a touch: Jacob, whom God promised to keep, was himself asleep when it was said. The name Israel can also be heard as Jacob renamed, the patriarch-turned-nation. The BBE's 'the eyes of Israel's keeper' adds 'eyes' that is not in the Hebrew.

philological_notes.note: A participle, 'one who keeps', a watchman or guard. It is the lead word of the psalm: keeper (v.3), keeper of Israel (v.4), keeps (v.5, 7, 8). The repetition is the structure.
'Slumber' and 'sleep'. Meiri reads the pair as an intensification, from the lightest lapse to full sleep; Radak says slumber is less than sleep.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH [is] your keeper; YHWH [is] your shade upon the hand of your right.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is your keeper. The LORD is your shade, standing at your right hand, as close as your own sword-arm, between you and the glare.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the psalm gives the keeper a name and a place. 'YHWH' is said twice, with the same short weight each time, like two taps on the shoulder. The first line says who he is, the second where he stands: 'upon the hand of your right', at the right side.

In the ancient Near East the right side was the place of the defender: the right hand held the weapon, the right was the open flank of a man carrying a shield on the left. A guardian at the right hand covers the exposed side. Metzudat David reads it exactly so: God shields the right hand in which a man does his work. The image of 'shade' is the sharpest in the verse. In a land of white sun, shade means life, the difference between a day's march and collapse. The KJV renders the Hebrew צֵל as 'shade' too, correctly, but 'upon thy right hand' suggests the shade lies on the hand; the Hebrew phrase עַל־יַד is closer to 'at the side of', as in 'at hand'. Meiri hears in the shade the shelter under God's wings.

philological_notes.note: 'Your shade'. A common image for protection in the Hebrew Bible; here it is a metaphor for God as the covering that keeps off the sun. Meiri extends it to shelter under his wings.
'At the hand of your right', the side of the defender. Radak says 'at your right hand, to help you in all your doings'.

verses.translation_literal: By day the sun will not strike you, nor the moon in the night.
verses.translation_dramatic: By day the sun will not strike you down. By night the moon will not touch you with harm. Under his shade the burning noon is bearable, and the cold white night lies harmless on the road.
verses.directors_commentary:
The shade of verse 5 now meets its enemy. The verb is the key: הִכָּה, 'to strike', 'to smite', the verb for a blow in battle. The KJV 'smite' gets this right and is closer than the BBE's soft 'touched', which loses the violence. In Israel the sun really does strike: the heat of summer noon can kill a traveller on an open road, and a story in 2 Kings 4:18–20 of a boy who cries 'my head!' in the harvest field is usually read as sunstroke.

The moon is the surprise. Why would the moon hurt anyone? The medieval commentators in the packet explain it with the medicine of their world: the sun dries the humours and the moon adds moisture and cold, and both cause disease (Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David). Others have suggested older beliefs in moon-sickness, or the moon as a god, but that claim has no source here. For the actors the pairing is simply total coverage: day and night, heat and chill. The two halves are also a merism, like 'heaven and earth', for 'at any hour'. Remember that in the surrounding cultures the sun and moon were gods; here they are only things that can hurt, and the LORD is greater than both.

philological_notes.note: 'It will strike you', the ordinary verb for a blow or a smiting, with a long old suffix form meaning 'you'. The sun is cast as an attacker.
'By day', an adverb. Paired with 'in the night' it makes a merism: all hours.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH will keep you from all harm; he will keep your life.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD will keep you from every evil. He will keep your life. All that you are, he will keep.
verses.directors_commentary:
The promise now widens from sun and moon to 'all harm', and the repeated verb 'keep' gathers it up in two short strokes. Say the second half lower and slower than the first; it is the most intimate line yet.

The KJV 'preserve thee from all evil' turns רָע, a word that means harm, misfortune or wrong, into the moral 'evil', and 'soul' for נֶפֶשׁ suggests the immortal soul of later theology. The Hebrew נֶפֶשׁ is the life, the self, the breathing person: throat, appetite, being. So the verse says 'he will keep your life', your whole living self, which Meiri reads as both body and inner life. Malbim in turn reads 'harm' as bodily evils and 'life' as guarding against sin. Radak gives it a plainer meaning: that people and wild beasts do not hurt you, and that you do not die of sickness. The shift of verb form is worth hearing: first 'he will keep you' (with the suffix), then 'he will keep' your life (with the object marker), a small echo that turns the promise inward.

philological_notes.note: 'Your life', the self. The KJV 'soul' carries later Greek and Christian weight; the Hebrew word is the whole living person. Radak reads it as not dying of illness; Malbim as guarding the self from sin.
'Harm', 'misfortune', as well as 'wrong'. In this context, with 'all', it is every kind of injury, from outside and within (Ibn Ezra).

verses.translation_literal: YHWH will keep your going out and your coming in, from now and until forever.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD will keep your going out and your coming in: every leaving, every returning, every threshold you will ever cross, from this hour and on, to the end of all ages.
verses.directors_commentary:
The last verse closes the circle: the psalm began with a person looking out at the horizon and ends with a promise over every doorway. 'Going out and coming in' is a Hebrew merism for the whole of life: leaving home for work or war and coming back to it. Ibn Ezra hears it as going out to battle and returning. Metzudat David reads it as not stumbling on the road in either direction. The KJV 'going out and thy coming in' is accurate and should be kept.

The verb 'keep' appears for the sixth time. It is deliberately repeated: six times in the psalm, like a fence of the same word around the traveller. The final phrase, מֵעַתָּה וְעַד־עוֹלָם, spans 'from now' to 'olam', an ancient word for a very long, hidden time, 'forever' or 'to the age'. The KJV 'from this time forth, and even for evermore' is an acceptable rendering though 'and even' adds a word the Hebrew lacks. Meiri notes that Deut 28:6 has the reverse order, 'blessed in your coming in, blessed in your going out'. In his reading, the psalm turns the blessing around because the speaker is an exile whose first step is going out of exile. For a staging, end on the word 'forever' held in the air, like the last note of a pilgrim's song, and then let the singer take the first step of the climb.

philological_notes.note: 'Your going out and your coming in', a merism for all of a person's activity. Meiri compares Deut 28:6, where the order is reversed, and reads the psalm as the exile's going out of exile and coming to the land.
A long, unmeasured time: 'forever', 'for the age'. Paired with 'from now', it spans the whole future.
